title: The US will ask the G20 not to build anything to govern AI
content:
The United States will ask the G20 not to build any new institutions for governing artificial intelligence. A White House official set out the position before a two-day meeting that opened in North Carolina on Tuesday, Reuters reported.
The argument is procedural rather than substantive, which is what makes it effective. Washington is not proposing rules it prefers; it is pressing member countries not to establish bodies that could write rules at all.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios are hosting.
The session is the first in a series running to the G20 leaders’ summit in Miami in December, which means the position set out this week is the one other countries will spend three months negotiating against.
The guest list tells you how the administration sees the subject. Sam Altman and Jensen Huang are attending in person and Elon Musk by video, which is an unusual composition for an intergovernmental meeting.
Canada has signalled it will push the other way, arguing for a balance between innovation and public trust and safety. China’s embassy did not say whether it would attend.
The G20 has no power to compel anybody, which cuts both ways. It cannot create a regulator, and the language it agrees still becomes the reference point national governments cite when they act at home.
The administration made the same case at the Paris AI summit, where JD Vance warned against paralysing the technology with regulation, and the US declined to sign an international statement on regulated AI use.
What has changed is the forum and the stakes. A G20 process produces communiqué language that shapes what national regulators believe they have licence to do, and an agreed sentence about international oversight is harder to unpick than a summit speech.
Europe arrives at this meeting having already built what the US is arguing against. The AI Act is in force, the Digital Services Act is being enforced against ChatGPT and other designated platforms, and the Cyber Resilience Act took effect this month.
The timing is awkward in another way. The chair of the Financial Stability Board told G20 finance ministers this week that AI-driven cyber risk is the most immediate threat to financial stability, and that warning came through exactly the kind of multilateral body the US wants left alone.
A United Nations panel has separately warned that AI development is outpacing both scientific understanding and government policy. That is the case for new institutions, made by an existing one.
For European regulators, the practical question is narrower than the principle. Nothing agreed in Miami would undo the AI Act, but a G20 consensus against international oversight makes European enforcement look like an outlier rather than a template.
The counter-argument deserves stating properly. Institutions built now would be designed around a technology nobody understands well, staffed by people appointed for a landscape that will have changed, and slow to correct once established.
There is also a competitive dimension nobody at the meeting will state plainly. A country hosting most of the leading model developers has less to gain from international oversight than countries that host none.
Developing economies have a different interest again, and a quieter one. Countries that neither build models nor regulate them effectively have most to gain from international standards and least capacity to insist on them.
Whether the position holds depends on who else wants a fight. The G20 works by consensus, and a communiqué that says nothing about AI governance is a win for the argument that nothing needs governing.
Miami is in December. Between now and then, the question is whether any member is willing to spend the diplomatic capital required to write a sentence the United States has said it will not accept.

report.summary: 美国拟推动G20不建立AI治理机构，反对新国际监管。
report.background: 美国在巴黎AI峰会已拒绝签署国际AI声明，本次在G20会议上再次提出不设新机构的立场，由商务部长和科技顾问主持。欧洲已实施AI法案等法规，形成鲜明对比。同时，金融稳定委员会警告AI网络风险，联合国也指出AI发展超出政策理解。G20无强制力，但共识语言会影响各国监管方向。
key_points: 美国主张G20不建立任何AI治理机构，理由是程序性的，即不应创设可制定规则的新实体。
G20共识虽无强制力，但会成为各国国内立法的参考，影响监管许可范围。
欧洲已通过AI法案等法规，与美方立场对立，美方反对可能使欧方成为异类。
金融稳定委员会警告AI网络风险是金融稳定最直接威胁，支持治理需求。
发展中国家希望国际标准，但缺乏推动能力，美国立场或使它们诉求更难实现。
report.impact: 对AI行业，美国立场可能减少监管障碍，加速技术发展，但增加安全风险。开发者将面临更模糊的合规环境，创新自由更大但责任也更重。普通用户可能更快享受AI进步，但需警惕潜在的网络风险与伦理问题。国际监管缺位可能导致各国规则碎片化，跨国企业协调成本上升。
report.tools: 关注OECD AI原则、欧盟AI法案合规工具，以及AI风险审计开源框架如AI Fairness 360、Responsible AI Toolbox，可帮助评估和缓解AI应用风险。
